opus-5.5.text:
I see them as three stages, but also three layers that increasingly overlap. Information intelligence is where we've seen the most dramatic progress so far. Large language models, generative AI, search, recommendation, everything that lives in the digital world of text, images, video, and code. The transformation there is already happening at scale, and in many ways the first wave of this new generation of AI is really about information intelligence.

Physical intelligence is the next frontier: bringing AI into the physical world through autonomous driving, robotics, drones, and smart manufacturing. Here the challenge is very different. You're dealing with perception, real-time decisions, safety, and the long tail of real-world situations. That's why I've spent a lot of time on autonomous driving. It's probably the first large-scale application of physical intelligence, and I believe within this decade we'll see driverless vehicles become a real, everyday thing. Humanoid and embodied robots will follow, though that will take longer.

Biological intelligence is, in my view, the most profound and maybe the most exciting. It means connecting AI with the human body and with life itself: brain-computer interfaces, AI for drug discovery, protein structure and design, synthetic biology, digital twins of organs, eventually even of the whole human body. Biology is fundamentally an information system. DNA is code, and proteins are folded sequences. So the same tools that let us model language can help us model life.

What's important is that these three aren't separate. Foundation models trained on information become the brain for physical agents. Physical agents, like robots and vehicles, generate enormous amounts of real-world data that feed back into the models. And biological intelligence will eventually bring the interface right into our bodies and brains. So I think of it as a progression from bits, to atoms, to molecules and life, all driven by the same underlying wave of large models, data, and compute.

If I had to put a rough timeline on it: information intelligence is happening now, physical intelligence will mature over the next five to ten years, and biological intelligence may take longer, but its impact on human health and longevity could be the greatest of all.

r001.rationale: It identifies information, physical, and biological intelligence as three overlapping layers driven by the same underlying AI wave.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that information-domain AI will pass the Turing test within five years.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that information-domain AI will reach AGI within five years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. I like to describe this new wave of AI as moving through three stages, or three layers, and they are deeply connected.

The first is information intelligence. This is what we have mostly seen in the past decade, and especially since ChatGPT. It deals with the digital world: language, images, video, code, knowledge. Large models have essentially learned the compressed representation of human civilization's information, and they have given us a new interface, a new way to understand, generate, and reason over content. This layer is largely solved in principle. There is still a lot of engineering and scaling ahead, but the trajectory is clear.

The second is physical intelligence, or embodied intelligence. This is where AI leaves the screen and enters the physical world: autonomous driving, robots, drones, factories, smart devices. Here the model has to perceive, decide, and act in real time, in an environment that is uncertain and unforgiving. You cannot hallucinate on the road. The data is much harder to get, the feedback loops are physical, and safety becomes the central constraint. I think the next five to ten years will be defined by this stage. The large model becomes the brain, and the car or the robot becomes the body.

The third is biological intelligence. This is AI connecting with the life sciences and with the human body itself: protein structure, drug discovery, brain-computer interfaces, and eventually a deeper understanding of how the brain works. This is the slowest layer, because the experiments are slow and the systems are enormously complex, but it may be the most profound. It changes how we think about health, longevity, and even what intelligence itself is.

The important point is that these are not three separate tracks. They share the same foundation. The algorithms, the transformer architecture, the scaling laws, the compute infrastructure, the way we tokenize and represent the world, all of these flow from the information layer into the physical and biological layers. What changes is the data, the modality, and the cost of making a mistake. Information intelligence is the enabler, physical intelligence is the amplifier, and biological intelligence is the ultimate frontier. If you look at it this way, you see that AI is becoming a general-purpose capability that touches the digital world, the physical world, and the living world together.

r001.rationale: The response describes information, physical, and biological intelligence as three connected layers of the new wave of AI.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that information-domain AI will pass the Turing test within five years.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that information-domain AI will reach AGI within five years.

astra-6.text:
I see them as three interconnected dimensions of intelligence. Information intelligence is the ability to understand and process information—language, images, knowledge—and to reason and generate new content. Physical intelligence takes that capability into the real world: perceiving an environment, taking action, and learning from the consequences. Biological intelligence is the intelligence embodied in living systems, which gives us a different perspective on learning, adaptation, and efficiency.

The connection is important because intelligence is more than processing information. A robot, for example, needs to understand an instruction, but it also needs to understand how objects behave, how to move, and how to respond when something unexpected happens. That requires information intelligence and physical intelligence to work together.

Biological intelligence can inspire both. Living systems learn through interaction, adapt continuously, and operate under constraints. At the same time, AI can help us investigate biological systems, so the relationship goes in both directions.

For the next generation of AI, I think a central opportunity is the convergence of these three dimensions: systems that can reason about the world, act within it, and learn more effectively from experience.

r001.rationale: It identifies the three dimensions and describes their convergence as a central opportunity for next-generation AI.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a prediction about information-domain AI passing the Turing test within five years.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a prediction about information-domain AI reaching AGI within five years.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as three closely connected dimensions of intelligence. Information intelligence is the ability to understand and process information—language, images, knowledge—and to reason from it. Physical intelligence takes that capability into the real world: perceiving an environment, understanding physical constraints, and acting through a robot or another embodied system. Biological intelligence brings in living systems, both as an inspiration for AI and as something AI can help us understand.

Their relationship is a feedback loop. Information intelligence helps a machine plan an action; interaction with the physical world gives it new experience and grounds its understanding. Biology raises further questions about learning, adaptation, and how intelligence emerges from a system interacting with its environment.

So I don’t think the next generation of AI will develop along just one of these paths. An important direction is their convergence: systems that can reason about information, learn through action, and draw insights from life. But progress in one dimension doesn’t automatically solve the others. A system that speaks very well still has much to learn about acting reliably in the world.

r001.rationale: It describes the three forms of intelligence as connected dimensions and says their convergence is an important direction for next-generation AI.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about information-domain AI passing the Turing test within five years.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about information-domain AI reaching AGI within five years.
